claim: The spike (S) protein is the main handle for SARS-CoV-2 to enter host cells via surface angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors.
source: The spike (S) protein is the main handle for SARS-CoV-2 to enter host cells via surface angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 infection mechanism, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: ACE2 binding enhances dynamics at a distal S1/S2 cleavage site and flanking protease docking site ~27 Å away.
source: Unexpectedly, ACE2 binding enhances dynamics at a distal S1/S2 cleavage site and flanking protease docking site ~27 Å away while dampening dynamics of the stalk hinge (central helix and heptad repeat [HR]) regions ~130 Å away.
evidence: This claim is supported by HDXMS experimental data showing increased deuterium exchange at these sites upon ACE2 binding.

claim: ACE2 binding dampens dynamics of the stalk hinge regions ~130 Å away from the binding site.
source: Unexpectedly, ACE2 binding enhances dynamics at a distal S1/S2 cleavage site and flanking protease docking site ~27 Å away while dampening dynamics of the stalk hinge (central helix and heptad repeat [HR]) regions ~130 Å away.
evidence: This is supported by HDXMS data showing decreased deuterium exchange in stalk regions upon ACE2 binding.

claim: The stalk and proteolysis sites of the S protein are dynamic hotspots in the prefusion state.
source: This highlights that the stalk and proteolysis sites of the S protein are dynamic hotspots in the prefusion state.
evidence: This is supported by HDXMS data showing high deuterium exchange in these regions.

claim: Protease docking sites flanking the S1/S2 cleavage site represent alternate allosteric hotspot targets for potential therapeutic development.
source: Thus, protease docking sites flanking the S1/S2 cleavage site represent alternate allosteric hotspot targets for potential therapeutic development.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the inference from the observed allosteric effects.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 belongs to the family of Coronaviridae, which includes other human pathogens including common cold-causing viruses (hCoV-OC43, HKU, and 229E), SARS, and MERS-CoV.
source: SARS-CoV-2 belongs to the family of Coronaviridae, which includes other human pathogens including common cold-causing viruses (hCoV-OC43, HKU, and 229E), SARS, and MERS-CoV (Corman et al., 2018; St-Jean et al., 2004; Lau et al., 2006; Warnes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on coronavirus classification.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has an ~30 kb RNA (positive stranded) genome with 14 open reading frames, encoding four structural proteins.
source: SARS-CoV-2 has an ~30 kb RNA (positive stranded) genome with 14 open reading frames, encoding four structural proteins – spike (S) protein, membrane (M) protein, envelope (E) protein, and nucleo-protein; 16 non-structural proteins, and 9 accessory proteins (Su et al., 2016; Andersen et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic characterization studies.

claim: An intact SARS-CoV-2 virion consists of a nucleocapsid core containing genomic RNA within a lipid–protein envelope forming a spherical structure of diameter ~100 nm.
source: An intact SARS-CoV-2 virion consists of a nucleocapsid core containing genomic RNA within a lipid–protein envelope forming a spherical structure of diameter ~100 nm (Ke et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural characterization studies.

claim: The viral envelope is decorated with S, M, and E proteins.
source: The viral envelope is decorated with S, M, and E proteins (Ke et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies.

claim: The prefusion S protein is a club-shaped homotrimeric class I viral fusion protein that has distinctive 'head' and 'stalk' regions.
source: The prefusion S protein is a club-shaped homotrimeric class I viral fusion protein that has distinctive 'head' and 'stalk' regions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1A and established knowledge.

claim: Upon host entry, the prefusion S protein is proteolyzed by host proteases into constituent S1 and S2 subunits.
source: A characteristic feature of SARS-CoV-2 is that upon host entry, its prefusion S protein is proteolyzed by host proteases into constituent S1 and S2 subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 infection mechanism.

claim: The S1 subunit comprises an N-terminal domain (NTD) and a receptor binding domain (RBD) that interacts with the host receptor angiotensin-converting enzyme-2 (ACE2).
source: The S1 subunit comprises an N-terminal domain (NTD) and a receptor binding domain (RBD) that interacts with the host receptor angiotensin-converting enzyme-2 (ACE2) (Lan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2020) to initiate viral entry into the target cell (Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and functional studies.

claim: Binding to ACE2 primes the S protein for proteolysis by host furin proteases at the S1/S2 cleavage site.
source: Binding to ACE2 primes the S protein for proteolysis by host furin proteases at the S1/S2 cleavage site (Walls et al., 2017; Vankadari, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on S protein proteolysis.

claim: The S2 subunit consists of six constituent domains harboring the membrane fusion machinery of the virus.
source: The S2 subunit consists of six constituent domains harboring the membrane fusion machinery of the virus. These comprise the fusion peptide (FP), heptad repeat (HR1), central helix (CH), heptad repeat 2 (HR2), connector domain (CD), transmembrane domain (TM), and cytoplasmic tail (CT) domain (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Extensive structural studies have captured S protein of coronaviruses in distinct open (PDB: 6VXX) and closed (PDB: 6VYB) conformational states relative to the orientation of the RBD.
source: Extensive structural studies (Ke et al., 2020; Walls et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020; Turoňová et al., 2020) have captured S protein of coronaviruses in distinct open (PDB: 6VXX) (Walls et al., 2020) and closed (PDB: 6VYB) (Walls et al., 2020) conformational states relative to the orientation of the RBD.
evidence: This is supported by citations to cryo-EM structural studies.

claim: A map of the S:ACE2 interface in solution and how ACE2 binding to the RBD primes enhanced proteolytic processing at the S1/S2 site is entirely unknown.
source: Despite extensive cryo-Electron Microscopy (cryo-EM) studies, a map of the S:ACE2 interface in solution and how ACE2 binding to the RBD primes enhanced proteolytic processing at the S1/S2 site is entirely unknown.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: Pepsin proteolysis of the S protein generated 317 peptides with high signal to noise ratios, yielding a primary sequence coverage of ~87%.
source: Pepsin proteolysis of the S protein generated 317 peptides with high signal to noise ratios, yielding a primary sequence coverage of ~87% (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from the HDXMS analysis.

claim: S protein is highly glycosylated (at least 22 sites have been predicted and characterized on S protein).
source: S protein is highly glycosylated (at least 22 sites have been predicted and characterized on S protein) (Watanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to glycosylation characterization studies.

claim: Of the 22 glycosylation sites, 20 sites are predicted to be N-linked glycosylation modifications.
source: Of these, 20 sites are predicted to be N-linked glycosylation modifications.
evidence: This is based on prediction and characterization from cited literature.

claim: Peptides spanning 12 of the 20 predicted glycosylation sites were obtained, and none of these peptides were glycosylated.
source: We obtained peptides spanning 12 of the 20 predicted glycosylation sites. None of these peptides were glycosylated, making deuterium exchange of non-glycosylated peptides the focus of this study.
evidence: This is experimental observation from the HDXMS analysis.

claim: The stalk region showed the greatest relative deuterium exchange at t = 1 and 10 min.
source: A deuterium exchange heat map (t = 1 and 10 min) revealed the stalk region to show the greatest relative deuterium exchange (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by HDXMS experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The stalk region shows at least 60° sweeping motions of the three identified hinge regions.
source: This is consistent with earlier studies showing at least 60° sweeping motions of the three identified hinge regions of the stalk (Turoňová et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural studies.

claim: MD simulations showed significant motions of the S protein ECD resulting from the high flexibility of the stalk region.
source: This was further verified via all-atom MD simulations of the S protein model embedded in a viral model membrane, which showed significant motions of the S protein ECD resulting from the high flexibility of the stalk region (Figure 2B), combined with large atomic fluctuations around the HR2 domain, compared to the rest of the protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in the figures.

claim: The S2 subunit showed higher average relative fractional deuterium uptake (~0.35) compared to the S1 subunit (~0.25) at early deuterium exchange time points.
source: Individually, S1 and S2 subunits showed different intrinsic deuterium exchange kinetics, where average relative fractional deuterium uptake (RFU) at early deuterium exchange time points of S1 subunit (~0.25) was lower than the average RFU (~0.35) for the S2 subunit (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, source data – Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from HDXMS analysis.

claim: Peptides connecting the RBD to the rest of the S protein showed greater deuterium exchange, suggesting a 'hinge' role for this segment.
source: Furthermore, peptides connecting the RBD to the rest of the S protein showed greater deuterium exchange, suggesting a 'hinge' role for this segment to facilitate RBD adopting an ensemble of open and closed conformational states (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference from HDXMS data about the functional role of this region.

claim: In simulations, the RBD oriented initially in an 'up' conformation exhibited spontaneous motion toward the 'down' conformation relative to the hinge region.
source: Indeed, in our simulations of the S protein (Figure 2B), the RBD oriented initially in an 'up' conformation and exhibited spontaneous motion toward the 'down' conformation relative to the hinge region (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Residues 476–486 in the receptor binding motif exhibited a higher degree of flexibility based on average atomic fluctuations.
source: Interestingly, a part of the receptor binding motif, specifically residues 476–486, exhibited a higher degree of flexibility based on its average atomic fluctuations (Figures 2B and 3B), suggesting a role for the ACE2 receptor in stabilizing S protein dynamics and priming it for host furin proteolysis.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and leads to an inference about ACE2's role.

claim: The NTD of the S protein showed low overall RFU (~0.2), consistent with its well-structured arrangement of β-sheets connected by loops.
source: The NTD of the S protein showed low overall RFU (~0.2), consistent with its well-structured arrangement of β-sheets connected by loops (Figures 1B and 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data from HDXMS that is consistent with structural knowledge.

claim: Certain regions of the NTD showed significantly higher deuterium exchange (~0.4), of which two loci (136–143, 243–265) span the dynamic interdomain interactions with the RBD.
source: Importantly, certain regions showed significantly higher deuterium exchange (~0.4), of which two loci (136–143, 243–265) span the dynamic interdomain interactions with the RBD.
evidence: This is experimental data from HDXMS analysis.

claim: High per-residue RMSFs and large principal motions were observed for residues 249–259 during simulations.
source: This is supported by the high per-residue root mean square fluctuations (RMSFs) and large principal motions observed for residues 249–259 during simulations (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Peptides spanning the region directly C-terminal to the S1/S2 cleavage site showed the greatest deuterium exchange (0.6).
source: Interestingly, peptides spanning the region directly C-terminal to the S1/S2 cleavage site showed the greatest deuterium exchange (0.6).
evidence: This is experimental data from HDXMS analysis.

claim: MD simulations revealed the unstructured loop housing the S1/S2 cleavage site (residues 677–689) to be highly dynamic with RMSFs reaching >1.0 nm.
source: Congruently, our MD simulations revealed the unstructured loop housing the S1/S2 cleavage site (residues 677–689) to be highly dynamic (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), with RMSFs reaching >1.0 nm.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data.

claim: The S1/S2 cleavage site has been abrogated in the construct of the S protein used in this study to block proteolytic processing into S1 and S2 subunits during expression in host cells.
source: It is important to note that the S1/S2 cleavage site has been abrogated in the construct of the S protein used in this study to block proteolytic processing into S1 and S2 subunits during expression in host cells.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental construct.

claim: Peptides forming the CH and CD showed lower deuterium exchange and lower RMSF values, suggesting their function as the central stable core of prefusion S.
source: We observed lower deuterium exchange (and lower RMSF values) at peptides forming the CH and CD, suggesting their function as the central stable core of prefusion S.
evidence: This is an inference from HDXMS and MD simulation data about functional roles.

claim: Peptides spanning hinge segments and heptad repeats (HR1 and HR2) showed high exchange and RMSF values, reflecting the S protein's ensemble properties.
source: In contrast, peptides spanning hinge segments and heptad repeats (HR1 and HR2) showed high exchange and RMSF values, reflecting the S protein's ensemble properties encompassing prefusion, fusion, and postfusion conformations in solution.
evidence: This is an inference from HDXMS and MD simulation data about conformational ensemble.

claim: A list of peptides common to RBDisolated and S protein showed differences in deuterium exchange only at interdomain interfaces within individual monomers and trimer interaction sites in the S protein.
source: A list of peptides common to RBDisolated and S protein ('RBDS') showed differences in deuterium exchange only at interdomain interfaces within individual monomers and trimer interaction sites in the S protein (Supplementary file 1: Table S3).
evidence: This is experimental data from comparative HDXMS analysis.

claim: Several RBDS peptides showed decreased exchange upon complexation with ACE2, including peptides 340–359, 400–420, 432–452, and 487–502.
source: Several RBDS peptides showed decreased exchange upon complexation with ACE2 (Figure 3). These include peptides 340–359, 400–420, 432–452, and 487–502 in the RBDS:ACE2 complex (Figure 4).
evidence: This is experimental data from HDXMS analysis of the complex.

claim: Sites showing deuterium exchange protection are consistent with the RBD:ACE2 interface described by X-ray crystallography (PDB: 6M0J).
source: Sites showing deuterium exchange protection are consistent with the RBD:ACE2 interface described by X-ray crystallography (PDB: 6M0J) (Lan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison of HDXMS data with structural data from cited literature.

claim: HDXMS revealed the core of the RBD:ACE2 interface to be contributed by peptides 340–359, 400–420, 432–452, and 491–510.
source: Further, HDXMS revealed the core of this interface to be contributed by peptides 340–359, 400–420, 432–452, and 491–510 (Figure 4A, D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is experimental data from HDXMS analysis.

claim: Loci showing large-magnitude differences in deuterium exchange correlate to certain mutational hotspots.
source: Interestingly, loci showing large-magnitude differences in deuterium exchange correlate to certain mutational hotspots (Wang et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is a correlation between HDXMS data and mutational data from cited literature.

claim: The magnitude of deuterium exchange protection was significantly more in RBDisolated than in RBDS, potentially reflecting the higher flexibility in the full-length S trimer relative to free RBD.
source: However, the magnitude of deuterium exchange protection was significantly more in RBDisolated than in RBDS, potentially reflecting the higher flexibility in the full-length S trimer relative to free RBD, interfering with ACE2 binding.
evidence: This is an inference from comparative HDXMS data about structural dynamics.

claim: High-resolution structures of RBD:ACE2 reveal the core of the RBD interface to be formed by amino acids Y449, Y453, N487, Y489, G496, T500, G502, Y505, L455, F456, F486, Q493, Q498, and N501.
source: High-resolution structures of RBD:ACE2 reveal the core of the RBD interface to be formed by amino acids Y449, Y453, N487, Y489, G496, T500, G502, Y505, L455, F456, F486, Q493, Q498, and N501 (Wang et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is structural information from cited literature.

claim: Cryo-EM studies have shown that each RBD in the trimeric S protein can adopt an open conformation irrespective of other RBDs, indicating an absence of cooperativity between the three RBDs within a trimer.
source: Cryo-EM studies have shown that each RBD in the trimeric S protein can adopt an open conformation irrespective of other RBDs, indicating an absence of cooperativity between the three RBDs within a trimer (Ke et al., 2020).
evidence: This is structural information from cited cryo-EM studies.

claim: ACE2 binding to RBDisolated and RBDS resulted in similar effects, with deuterium exchange protection at the peptide regions spanning the known binding interface of RBD.
source: ACE2 binding to RBDisolated and RBDS resulted in similar effects, where we observed deuterium exchange protection at the peptide regions spanning the known binding interface of RBD.
evidence: This is experimental data from comparative HDXMS analysis.

claim: Increased deuterium exchange was observed at the hinge region upon ACE2 binding, indicating allosteric conformational changes associated with restricting the open and closed states interconversion.
source: Notably, increased deuterium exchange was observed at the hinge region (Figure 3D), indicating allosteric conformational changes, associated with restricting the open and closed states interconversion.
evidence: This is an inference from HDXMS data about allosteric effects.

claim: The destabilization/local unfolding observed at the hinge region as a result of ACE2 binding enables RBD to maintain the open conformation.
source: Therefore, the destabilization/local unfolding observed at the hinge region as a result of ACE2 binding enables RBD to maintain the open conformation.
evidence: This is an inference from HDXMS data about the mechanism of conformational stabilization.

claim: Small molecules and biologics targeting the hinge region to lock RBD in the closed state would be of potential high therapeutic value.
source: It therefore seems likely that small molecules and biologics targeting the hinge region to lock RBD in the closed state would be of potential high therapeutic value.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the observed dynamics.

claim: ACE2 binding at the RBD induced large-scale changes in deuterium exchange in distal regions of the S protein.
source: Unexpectedly, ACE2 binding at the RBD induced large-scale changes in deuterium exchange in distal regions of the S protein.
evidence: This is experimental data from HDXMS analysis showing allosteric effects.

claim: Some peptides in the stalk of S protein showed decreased exchange in the S:ACE2 complex, indicating that ACE2 receptor interactions stabilized the hinge dynamics in the S protein.
source: Some of the peptides in the stalk of S protein showed decreased exchange in the S:ACE2 complex (Figure 4C,D). This indicates that ACE2 receptor interactions stabilized the hinge dynamics in the S protein.
evidence: This is an inference from HDXMS data about allosteric stabilization.

claim: Decreased exchange was seen in distal sites in the S2 subunit, localized at the FP locus and CH.
source: Decreased exchange was also seen in the distal sites in the S2 subunit, localized at the FP locus and CH.
evidence: This is experimental data from HDXMS analysis.

claim: Increased exchange was seen in multiple peptides flanking the S1/S2 cleavage site, HR1 domain, and critically at the S1/S2 cleavage site.
source: Interestingly, increased exchange was seen in multiple peptides flanking the S1/S2 cleavage site, HR1 domain, and critically at the S1/S2 cleavage site (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is experimental data from HDXMS analysis.

claim: Even though the protease cleavage site is abrogated in the construct used in this study, increased dynamics were observed as inferred by the higher relative deuterium exchange at the S1/S2 locus.
source: Even though the protease cleavage site is abrogated in the construct used in this study, we still observed increased dynamics as inferred by the higher relative deuterium exchange at the S1/S2 locus.
evidence: This is experimental observation from HDXMS analysis.

claim: The S1/S2 region exhibited high RMSF values during simulations.
source: Furthermore, this region exhibited high RMSF values during simulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data.

claim: ACE2 binding induces allosteric enhancement of dynamics at the S1/S2 locus, providing mechanistic insights into the conformational switch from the prefusion to fusogenic intermediate.
source: These results clearly indicate that ACE2 binding induces allosteric enhancement of dynamics at this locus, providing mechanistic insights into the conformational switch from the prefusion to fusogenic intermediate.
evidence: This is an inference from HDXMS and MD simulation data about the mechanism.

claim: ACE2 binding allosterically primes HR1 and other high exchanging regions flanking the S1/S2 cleavage site for enhanced furin protease binding and cleavage.
source: This suggests that ACE2 binding allosterically primes HR1 and other high exchanging regions flanking the S1/S2 cleavage site for enhanced furin protease binding and cleavage.
evidence: This is an inference from HDXMS data about the mechanism of proteolytic priming.

claim: The S1/S2 cleavage site is a critical hotspot for S protein dynamic transitions for facilitating SARS-CoV-2's entry into the host.
source: Importantly, these results suggest that the S1/S2 cleavage site is a critical hotspot for S protein dynamic transitions for facilitating SARS-CoV-2's entry into the host, and therefore represents a new target for inhibitory therapeutics against the virus.
evidence: This is an inference and speculation based on the observed dynamics.

claim: Previous studies have shown that 14 key amino acids of RBD interact with ACE2, wherein mutations at six sites resulted in higher binding affinity of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Previous studies have shown that 14 key amino acids of RBD interact with ACE2, wherein mutations at six sites resulted in higher binding affinity of SARS-CoV-2 (Li et al., 2005).
evidence: This is information from cited literature on binding interactions.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 adopted a different binding mode to ACE2 as a superior strategy for infection compared to SARS-CoV-1.
source: SARS-CoV-2 adopted a different binding mode to ACE2 as a superior strategy for infection compared to SARS-CoV-1.
evidence: This is established knowledge from comparative studies of SARS viruses.

claim: A crystal structure of RBDisolated:ACE2 complex has identified 24 key ACE2 residues, spanning across peptides 16–45, 79–83, 325–330, 350–357, and R393.
source: A crystal structure of RBDisolated:ACE2 complex has identified 24 key ACE2 residues, spanning across peptides 16–45, 79–83, 325–330, 350–357, and R393 (Towler et al., 2004).
evidence: This is structural information from cited crystallography studies.

claim: R393 and residues 325–330 are unique to SARS-CoV-1 interaction with ACE2.
source: While most of these residues are conserved in binding to both SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2, R393 and residues 325–330 are unique to SARS-CoV-1 interaction (Wang et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is information from cited comparative binding studies.

claim: Increased deuterium exchange was observed at residues R393 and 325–330 in the S:ACE2 complex compared to ACE2 alone.
source: Interestingly, we observed increased deuterium exchange at these residues in the S:ACE2 complex compared to ACE2 alone (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is experimental data from HDXMS analysis.

claim: A reduction in deuterium exchange was observed across both RBDisolated:ACE2 and larger S:ACE2 complexes compared to free ACE2.
source: We observed a reduction in deuterium exchange across both RBDisolated:ACE2 and larger S:ACE2 complexes compared to free ACE2 (Figure S8B and S8C).
evidence: This is experimental data from HDXMS analysis.

claim: RBD binding stabilizes ACE2 globally, specifically showing large differences at the binding site (peptides 21–29, 30–39, and 75–92), and also at distal regions (peptides 121–146, 278–292, and 575–586).
source: Differences in deuterium exchange between RBDisolated:ACE2 complex and free ACE2 showed that RBD binding stabilizes ACE2 globally, specifically large differences at the binding site (peptides 21–29, 30–39, and 75–92), and also at distal regions (peptides 121–146, 278–292, and 575–586) from the RBD binding site of ACE2 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is experimental data from HDXMS analysis showing binding and allosteric effects.

claim: Cryo-EM studies have shown that a dimeric full-length ACE2 receptor can stably bind to one trimer of the S protein.
source: Cryo-EM studies have shown that a dimeric full-length ACE2 receptor can stably bind to one trimer of the S protein (Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is structural information from cited cryo-EM studies.

claim: A combination of HDXMS and MD simulations provides a close-up of S protein dynamics in the prefusion, ACE2-bound, and other associated conformations.
source: Here, a combination of HDXMS and MD simulations provides a close-up of S protein dynamics in the prefusion, ACE2-bound, and other associated conformations.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the methodological approach and findings.

claim: ACE2 binding to the isolated RBD and S protein alike leads to binding and stabilization.
source: ACE2 binding to the isolated RBD and S protein alike leads to binding and stabilization.
evidence: This is a summary of HDXMS findings.

claim: ACE2 binding to the RBD induces global conformational changes across the entire S trimer.
source: Interestingly, ACE2 binding to the RBD induces global conformational changes across the entire S trimer.
evidence: This is a summary of HDXMS findings showing allosteric effects.

claim: The stalk region undergoes dampening of conformational motions while showing increased deuterium exchange at the proteolytic processing sites upon ACE2 binding.
source: Importantly, the stalk region undergoes dampening of conformational motions while showing increased deuterium exchange at the proteolytic processing sites.
evidence: This is a summary of HDXMS findings.

claim: This study may help in explaining how mutations in emerging strains in the ongoing COVID-19 outbreak might alter dynamics and allostery of ACE2 binding.
source: This study may help in explaining how mutations in emerging strains in the ongoing COVID-19 outbreak might alter dynamics and allostery of ACE2 binding and offer a mechanistic basis for altered infectivities observed in emerging strains.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the findings.

claim: Sites on S protein showing altered deuterium exchange describe allosteric propagation of ACE2 binding and represent novel cryptic targets for therapeutic small molecule inhibitor/antibody discovery.
source: Sites on S protein showing altered deuterium exchange describe allosteric propagation of ACE2 binding and represent novel cryptic targets for therapeutic small molecule inhibitor/antibody discovery.
evidence: This is an inference and speculation based on the observed allosteric effects.

claim: Mutations were introduced at the RRAR motif at the S1/S2 cleavage site (682–685) which was substituted by GSAS.
source: Mutations were introduced into this construct at two sites: (i) RRAR motif at the S1/S2 cleavage site (682–685) was substituted by GSAS and (ii) KV motif (986–987) was substituted with two prolines.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the construct design.

claim: KV motif (986–987) was substituted with two prolines.
source: Mutations were introduced into this construct at two sites: (i) RRAR motif at the S1/S2 cleavage site (682–685) was substituted by GSAS and (ii) KV motif (986–987) was substituted with two prolines.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the construct design.

claim: S (1–1208), ACE2, and RBD eluted as trimers, dimers, and monomers, respectively, on size-exclusion chromatography.
source: S (1–1208), ACE2, and RBD eluted as trimers, dimers, and monomers, respectively, on size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from size-exclusion chromatography.

claim: Isolated RBD constructs showed high-affinity binding to ACE2.
source: Isolated RBD constructs showed high-affinity binding to ACE2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from binding assays.

claim: S:ACE2 and RBDisolated:ACE2 complexes have KD of ~15 and ~150 nM, respectively.
source: S:ACE2 and RBDisolated:ACE2 complexes (KD of ~15 and ~150 nM, respectively) (Wrapp et al., 2020) were pre-incubated at 37°C for 30 min in a 1:1 molar ratio to achieve >90% binding prior to each hydrogen–deuterium exchange reaction.
evidence: This is binding affinity data cited from literature.

claim: An integrative model of full-length SARS-CoV-2 S protein was built using Modeller v.9.21.
source: An integrative model of full-length SARS-CoV-2 S protein was built using Modeller v.9.21 (Šali and Blundell, 1993).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about model building.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of prefusion S ECD in the open conformation (PDB: 6VSB) was used as the template for the ECD.
source: The cryo-EM structure of prefusion S ECD in the open conformation (PDB: 6VSB) (Wrapp et al., 2020) was used as the template for the ECD with missing loops on the NTD and the C-terminus of the ECD modeled based on the cryo-EM structure of S ECD in the closed conformation resolved at a higher resolution (PDB: 6XR8) (Cai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about model building using structural templates.

claim: Palmitoylation was performed at three cysteine residues (C1236, C1240, and C1243) on the CT domain based on a study showing its importance in SARS S protein function.
source: Palmitoylation was performed at three cysteine residues (C1236, C1240, and C1243) on the CT domain based on a study showing its importance in SARS S protein function (Petit et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a methodological detail based on cited literature.

claim: The S protein model was embedded into a model membrane representing the endoplasmic reticulum–Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC).
source: The S protein model was then embedded into a model membrane representing the endoplasmic reticulum–Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) (van Meer, 1998), where coronaviruses are known to assemble in a bud form (Krijnse-Locker et al., 1994; Klumperman et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a methodological detail based on cited knowledge about coronavirus assembly.

claim: All-atom MD simulation was performed for 200 ns using GROMACS 2018 and the CHARMM36 force field.
source: All-atom MD simulation was performed for 200 ns using GROMACS (University of Groningen, Netherlands) 2018 (Abraham et al., 2015) and the CHARMM36 force field (Huang and MacKerell, 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about simulation parameters.

claim: The system was solvated with 590,742 TIP3P water molecules and 0.15 M NaCl salt, achieved by adding 3235 Na+ and 2103 Cl- ions.
source: The system was solvated with 590,742 TIP3P water molecules and 0.15 M NaCl salt, achieved by adding 3235 Na+ and 2103 Cl- ions.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about simulation system setup.

claim: For simulations of the ACE2 receptor, the cryo-EM structure of the ACE2-B0AT1 complex in the open conformation (PDB: 6M1D) was used.
source: For simulations of the ACE2 receptor, the cryo-EM structure of the ACE2-B0AT1 complex in the open conformation (PDB: 6M1D) (Yan et al., 2020) was used.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the structural template used.

claim: Simulations of the ACE2 dimer complexed with the B0AT1 amino acid transporter in a model epithelial membrane revealed a large motion of the peptidase domain.
source: Simulations of the ACE2 dimer complexed with the B0AT1 amino acid transporter (PDB: 6M1D) (Yan et al., 2020) in a model epithelial membrane revealed a large motion of the peptidase domain, which recognizes the S protein RBD, with respect to the transmembrane and juxtamembrane domains (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is data from MD simulations.

claim: The large motion of the ACE2 peptidase domain is reminiscent of the flexible tilting displayed by the S protein ECD itself.
source: This large motion is reminiscent of the flexible tilting displayed by the S protein ECD itself, suggesting that both S protein and ACE2 have adaptable hinges that allow for orientational freedom of the domains involved in recognition.
evidence: This is an inference from MD simulation data comparing dynamics of S protein and ACE2.
